social.label: New social history
social.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.
social.representative_figures_and_works: E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). Geoff Eley and Keith Nield: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980).

social.scope_note: Class formation, demographic reconstruction, communities, and everyday life have different methods; Marxist history is one substantial component. The 1950s–1970s label marks expansion, not termination: later mapped works extend and dispute these programmes. Earlier women’s social inquiry remains visible as comparison. Neither one European class trajectory nor transparent experience supplies a universal model; critical interventions do not erase productive inheritances.

strands.works: The Making of the English Working Class; The Chartists; Work, Culture, and Society

strands.works: Cambridge Group population and household studies

strands.works: Poverty and Progress (1964)

strands.works: Family Fortunes (1987)

strands.title: Colonial labor and contested categories
strands.focus: Chakrabarty questions universal class narratives through Bengal jute workers; Cooper examines colonial labor classifications and African social relations. Neither supplies one model for all colonized workers.
strands.works: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Experience, identities and historical explanation
strands.focus: Read Scott’s critique of foundational experience alongside Thompson’s historical class formation. Scott’s proposed historicization is not a consensus or a demand to abandon experience.
strands.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

strands.title: Peasant movements, belief and political aims
strands.focus: Hilton compares 1381 with continental movements while examining aims, allies and outcomes. Conflict does not mean constant open warfare; economic/social relations require political and religious analysis. Neither quick defeat nor later change settles causation.
strands.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973), selected introduction and conclusion

strands.title: Bandit narratives, political power and local research
strands.focus: Hobsbawm’s revised model responds to myth and patronage objections and draws on Colombian scholarship. Songs are mediated evidence; political actors and social settings cannot be inferred directly from heroic stories.
strands.works: Bandits (1969; revised edition 2000); Sánchez/Meertens (1987)

strands.title: Migration and the timing of observation
strands.focus: Ferrie’s response to Thernstrom asks who disappears from a local sample and what happens before its first observation. His male immigrant sample does not represent every worker or family.
strands.works: Ferrie (1996 manuscript),1–8,21

strands.title: Culture under capitalism: continuity or reworking?
strands.focus: Chakrabarty rejects deriving workers’ culture from economic function alone. Nair asks whether describing traditions as survivals makes them too fixed, and how their reworking within capitalism should enter the explanation.
strands.works: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989/2000), preface xi–xv; Nair review (1990), 98

strands.title: Separate spheres: categories, chronology and regional evidence
strands.focus: Davidoff and Hall connect class formation to gender and familial support. Vickery values their detailed research but questions its chronology and generalization: her Lancashire comparison crosses land and trade, while prescriptive language does not straightforwardly establish women’s confinement.
strands.works: Family Fortunes (1987), prologue opening; Vickery (1993), 393–401

strands.title: Experience, agency and changing discourse
strands.focus: Canning accepts the need to historicize experience but questions treating identity recovery and analysis of difference as alternatives. She asks how subjects reinterpret or transform discourse; this is a sympathetic criticism of Scott, not a return to self-evident experience.
strands.works: Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Canning (1994), 374–378

strands.title: Politics within social-history debate
strands.focus: Eley and Nield asked in 1980 why social history ignored politics (article unread; they recalled in 2007 that it 'drew disappointingly little response in print' and that they had been 'trying to create a space for political analysis in the expanded sense given to "politics" by the politics of knowledge of 1968', 2000, p. 14). Joyce's 'The End of Social History?' (1995; unread) drew their 'Starting Over' (1995; unread), which Joyce said equated his questioning of social history 'with contemporary neo-liberalism' (1996). In 'Farewell to the Working Class?' (2000, read in full) they held that 'class discursively understood … is a better starting point' while wanting 'to break this logic of disavowal' (p. 16); Scott's reply (read in full) called this 'Assent to Discourse' and objected that insisting on class forecloses other political categories (p. 69); Cooper answered that 'they did not think to ask Karl Marx' (p. 61). The debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980), coauthored; “Starting Over” (1995); “Farewell to the Working Class?” and reply (ILWCH 57, 2000); The Future of Class in History (2007)

conceptual.label: Conceptual history / Begriffsgeschichte
conceptual.description: Traces changing political and social concepts in relation to historical experience, conflict, and expectations. Koselleck links conceptual change to different temporalities and to the emergence of modern historical consciousness. This overlaps with contextual intellectual history while asking different questions about semantic change across time. Collective German lexicon work, French studies of polemical usages and Richter’s comparisons represent distinct programs. Concepts can register and help shape social processes without exhausting those processes.
conceptual.representative_figures_and_works: Reinhart Koselleck, Vergangene Zukunft (1979), translated as Futures Past (1985; Columbia edition 2004). The German conceptual-history tradition is related to, but not a branch of, Skinner and Pocock’s Cambridge School.

representative_people.context: German conceptual history; not a branch of the Cambridge School. Separates words from concepts, concepts from social reality and analytical categories from historical actors’ vocabulary; experience and expectation organize questions rather than determine their answers.
representative_people.works: Vergangene Zukunft (1979); Futures Past (1985)

conceptual.scope_note: Koselleck’s conceptual change and historical time differ from reconstructing a particular author’s intervention. Brunner, Conze and Koselleck’s editorial association does not imply identical methods or political commitments. Experience and expectation are formal research categories with variable contents; the proposed modern temporal transformation is neither a universal timetable nor a prediction of particular events.

strands.title: Words, concepts and overlapping semantic layers
strands.focus: The same word can persist while conceptual content changes; a concept can carry multiple historical layers. Koselleck combines synchronic usage with diachronic comparison without treating every word as a key historical concept.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Concepts as indicators and factors
strands.focus: Concepts register social relations and can help act upon them, but social events are not identical with their linguistic conceptualization. Historians must also distinguish actors’ terms from their own justified analytical categories.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Experience, expectation and unequal temporalities
strands.focus: These formal categories direct questions about remembered pasts and anticipated futures. Their asymmetry does not independently predict contents; Koselleck’s modernity thesis recognizes simplification, unequal social temporalities and recurring structures.
strands.works: Futures Past, preface and selected chapter 14 pp. 255–264, 271–275

strands.title: Collective lexicon, distinct programs and political criticism
strands.focus: Brunner, Conze and Koselleck participate in one editorial project with different research emphases. Criticism of Brunner’s political framing and textual revisions must be attributed and assessed through evidence, without assigning a uniform position to all editors and contributors.
strands.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe; Koselleck’s preface and Tribe’s selected introduction

strands.title: French social roles and opposing uses
strands.focus: Gumbrecht and Reichardt investigate philosophe as a social role. Opponents can use similar semantic contents with opposed force; dictionaries participate in polemics instead of neutrally settling every usage. Their court discussion explicitly draws on Elias.
strands.works: Philosophe, Philosophie, Handbuch Heft 3 (1985), pp. 7–14

strands.title: Comparing conceptual history and political languages
strands.focus: Richter’s 1995 comparison makes differences among the German lexicon, French Handbuch and Skinner/Pocock programs explicit. Shared historical vocabulary questions do not establish one method or an origin of one school in another.
strands.works: The History of Political and Social Concepts (1995), chapters 4 and 6, abstracts

strands.title: Public opinion and contested sovereignty
strands.focus: Goldman distinguishes appeals to an enlightened general will from the divergent opinions of provinces. The meaning of public opinion changes within struggles over who can speak for a sovereign people.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 15–20; earlier joint presentation acknowledged in note 26

demography.label: Historical demography & history of the family
demography.description: Combines related inquiries into population, households, childhood and intimate relations. Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s aggregate and household studies differ from Ariès’s historical concepts and Stone’s family interpretation. Pollock’s criticism questions evidence and sweeping changes in parental care. Lee and Wang’s Chinese population study challenges received Malthusian comparisons without making the field’s regional patterns uniform.
demography.representative_figures_and_works: Louis Henry; Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (1964); Peter Laslett, The World We Have Lost (1965); Wrigley and Schofield, The Population History of England (1981); Philippe Ariès (1960); Lawrence Stone (1977). Additional selections: Hajnal (1965); Laslett and Wall (1972); Pollock (1981/1983); Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997); Lee and Wang (1999).

demography.scope_note: Family reconstitution and aggregate reconstruction differ from histories of childhood or family meanings; Henry, Annales, and Cambridge are not interchangeable. Household composition, marriage behavior, concepts of childhood and parental conduct are different objects of study. England and France are prominent in this selection; Chinese comparative research broadens the questions without representing all non-European family histories. Later institutional webpages are retrospective sources, not an extension beyond 2000.

strands.title: Family change, social differences and source selection

ethnohistory.label: Ethnohistory
ethnohistory.date_label: Earlier interdisciplinary work · Great Lakes–Ohio Valley project 1953 · Lurie 1961 · continuing regional programmes
ethnohistory.description: Combines historical and anthropological inquiry through archives, material evidence, language, oral traditions and situated cultural interpretation. North American claims research, Wendat/Huron historical reconstruction, Nahua documentary studies and Andean historical anthropology form distinct programmes. Ethnohistory studies historical change rather than assigning some peoples to an unchanging ethnographic past.

Trigger: The Children of Aataentsic (1976; later preface 1987); James Lockhart: The Nahuas After the Conquest (1992); John V. ethnohistory.scope_note: The field overlaps with Indigenous history but does not automatically confer Indigenous authority, community consent or decolonizing method. Claims research could serve governments as well as claimants. Indigenous authors appear here as qualified interlocutors and critics, not as members of an externally assigned school. Lurie herself disputes restricting the approach to particular peoples. The Americas dominate this initial selection; Vansina provides a comparison with African oral-tradition methodology, not proof that African history descends from US ethnohistory.

racial_formation.label: Racial formation
racial_formation.description: Investigates how racial categories and meanings are produced and contested through social, political and economic relations. Omi and Winant’s programme treats race as historically specific and consequential, not as a biological essence or a simple expression of another social category.
racial_formation.scope_note: A distinct theoretical programme relevant to histories of racialization, not a synonym for Black history or all scholarship about race. Original 1986 and revised 1994 editions remain distinct. The checked course extract is labelled second edition; its retyped pagination and edition attribution have not been independently authenticated. Intersectional analysis connects racial inquiry with gender, class and sexuality without being identical to racial-formation theory.
